result: Aedes aegypti is a major disease vector responsible for transmitting multiple arboviruses and placing approximately half the world's population at risk, causing an estimated 390 million dengue infections annually.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 establish the public health significance of Ae. aegypti as a disease vector. All three claims are supported by appropriate citations to peer-reviewed literature (Scott and Takken, 2012; Bhatt et al., 2013), providing a well-established foundation for the study's motivation.

result: Traditional and current mosquito control methods have limitations including development of resistance, high costs, environmental impacts, and requirements for continuous application, motivating the need for novel control technologies.
evaluation: Claims C4-C11 provide context for existing control methods and their limitations. These claims are well-supported by citations to relevant literature and establish the rationale for developing gene drive technologies. The claims about Wolbachia effectiveness variability (C11) are particularly well-documented with multiple citations.

result: CRISPR-based homing gene drives have been successfully developed in multiple organisms but not yet in Ae. aegypti, representing a gap in vector control technology.
evaluation: Claims C12-C22 establish the state of gene drive technology prior to this work. The claims are well-supported by extensive citations documenting gene drive development in other species (yeast, flies, mice, Anopheles species) and correctly identify the absence of such systems in Ae. aegypti (C22), establishing the novelty of the current work.

result: The white gene was selected as a drive target due to its screenable phenotype, and a highly conserved gRNA target sequence (100% conserved across 143 wild populations) was identified that achieved 92.7 ± 5.8% mutation efficiency in injection experiments.
evaluation: Claims C27-C29 describe rational target selection. C28 is supported by bioinformatic analysis of 143 wild mosquitoes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B), demonstrating target conservation. C29 is supported by experimental injection data showing high mutation efficiency, validating the target site accessibility and gRNA activity.

result: Four U6 promoters (U6a-d) were functionally characterized for gRNA expression in Ae. aegypti, showing somatic mutation frequencies of 32.5-71.3% and germline mutation rates of 27.6-67.5%, with U6b and U6c achieving up to 100% somatic knockout when combined with ubiq-Cas9.
evaluation: Claims C30-C32 and C67-C71 describe the characterization of U6 promoters, which had not been functionally tested in Ae. aegypti prior to this work (C69). The experimental data (Figure 1B, 1C) support the reported mutation frequencies. This represents a significant technical advance enabling gene drive development in this species.

result: Split gene drives with unlinked Cas9 and gRNA components were successfully engineered in Ae. aegypti, achieving cleavage rates up to 100% and homing rates as high as 94%.
evaluation: Claims C23-C25 and C55 describe the core achievement of the study. The split drive design is supported by appropriate citations (C23), and the reported cleavage and homing rates are supported by experimental data throughout the Results section. C72 notes an unexpected insertion in one construct, demonstrating appropriate quality control.

result: The white gene exhibits sex-linked inheritance due to its proximity to the male-determining factor Nix on chromosome I, resulting in sex-biased transmission patterns in males but normal Mendelian inheritance when both sexes are considered.
evaluation: Claims C33-C35 establish the genetic basis for observed inheritance patterns, supported by multiple citations. Claims C73-C75 report experimental observations consistent with this genetic architecture. The sex-biased transmission in males (C74) is well-documented experimentally (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and the overall 50% transmission rate (C75) confirms Mendelian inheritance.

result: Split drive performance varied by Cas9 promoter, with wU6b-GDe/w+; nup50-Cas9/+ showing the best performance: 100% somatic mosaicism and 80.5 ± 5.0% inheritance in females, and 51.0 ± 3.9% mosaicism and 66.9 ± 5.4% inheritance in males, demonstrating that homing and cleavage efficiencies depend on timing and expression of drive components.
evaluation: Claims C36-C42 and C56 report systematic testing of different Cas9 promoters. The data are well-documented in Figures 3B-F and supplementary files. The variation in performance across different promoter combinations (C56) is supported by the experimental comparisons. The best-performing system (nup50-Cas9) shows super-Mendelian inheritance in both sexes.

result: The split-drive systems showed relatively stable cleavage and transmission rates over multiple generations, with the wU6b-GDe/w+; nup50-Cas9/+ system maintaining drive activity in males across generations.
evaluation: Claims C43, C79, and C80 address multi-generational stability. C43 is supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing stability across generations. C79 and C80 demonstrate differential performance between exu-Cas9 and nup50-Cas9 systems in males, with nup50-Cas9 maintaining drive activity. The data support the conclusion of relative stability.

result: Maternal deposition of Cas9 results in embryonic cleavage activity and generation of drive-resistant alleles at low frequency (0.31 ± 0.07%), with resistance alleles containing indels at the gRNA target site.
evaluation: Claims C44, C57, C76-C78, and C81-C83 describe maternal carryover effects and resistant allele generation. C44 quantifies resistant allele frequency with experimental data (Supplementary file 5b). C82 provides molecular characterization (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). C83 appropriately contextualizes this as a known issue in gene drive systems with supporting citations.

result: Female fecundity was significantly reduced in nup50-Cas9 and wU6b-GDe/nup50-Cas9 lines compared to wild-type, likely due to Cas9 toxicity, while other fitness parameters showed no significant differences.
evaluation: Claims C45 and C84 report fitness assessment results supported by Supplementary file 7a. C46 and C86 provide context from the literature about Cas9 toxicity. C85 offers a reasonable inference connecting germline Cas9 expression to reduced fecundity. The fitness cost is specific to Cas9-expressing lines, supporting the toxicity hypothesis.

result: Mathematical modeling predicts that 10 consecutive weekly releases of 10,000 homozygous split drive males can drive the system to ~97% frequency in the release population, remaining above 87% for three years, with limited spread to neighboring populations (~30% peak frequency), demonstrating confinability and reversibility.
evaluation: Claims C26 and C47-C53 describe modeling predictions supported by Figure 4A and related figures. The modeling uses experimentally determined parameters (Supplementary file 7b) and the MGDrivE framework. C87 demonstrates the advantage over inundative releases (Figure 4B). The predictions are internally consistent and appropriately parameterized based on experimental data.

result: A hypothetical linked homing drive would spread more extensively than the split drive, reaching >67% frequency in neighboring populations after a single release, but would be outnumbered by resistant alleles within four years.
evaluation: Claims C88-C90 compare split drive to linked drive systems using modeling. The predictions are supported by Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C. C89 appropriately suggests strategies to reduce resistant allele generation, supported by citations. The comparison demonstrates the confinability advantage of split drives.

result: The reversal of the split drive system can be accelerated by releasing wild-type males.
evaluation: Claim C91 describes a strategy for accelerating drive reversal. This is a logical inference from the modeling framework and is consistent with the split drive design where fitness costs and component separation lead to natural decline. The claim is reasonable given the system's properties.

result: Current antiviral effectors have limitations including difficulty in multiplexing and viral mutation, and gene drive efficiencies are impacted by multiple factors, but split drive technologies offer a responsible approach for field testing due to their confinability and reversibility.
evaluation: Claims C58-C63 discuss limitations of current effectors and advantages of split drives. C58-C60 are supported by appropriate citations. C61 summarizes established knowledge about factors affecting drive efficiency. C62 and C63 make reasonable inferences about the value of split drives for field testing, though C63 is somewhat speculative about real-world performance.

result: All experiments used the Ae. aegypti Liverpool strain, which is the strain used to generate the reference genome sequences.
evaluation: Claims C64 and C65 describe the mosquito strain used in experiments. These are straightforward methodological statements supported by citations (Matthews et al., 2018; Nene et al., 2007). Using the reference strain is appropriate for this proof-of-concept work.
